body: Taking the lock only around the map write means two goroutines can now build the same key at once. For example, `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` can race with an init worker, or two watch events for a new namespace/resource can arrive close together. Before, `BuildIndex` was serialized, so this couldn't happen. Now both callers build a full index. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) they both call `bleve.New` on the same `dir`, so one fails or they corrupt each other's files. The last writer overwrites `b.cache[key]`, and the losing index is never closed, which leaks file handles and memory. Writes that went to the losing index are silently lost. The lock should be per key (singleflight or a per-key mutex / building-in-progress entry), not removed.

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it at the end of `searchSupport.init`. It is also called from the Prometheus `Collect` path (`BleveIndexMetrics`). Either call can run while the watch goroutine in `handleEvent`/`getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex` writes `b.cache[key]`. Now that the write is under a narrower lock, and startup runs many builds concurrently, a concurrent map read/write is more likely. Go treats that as a fatal error that crashes the process, not a recoverable panic. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` here.

`s.search.TotalDocs()` is called here after the watch goroutine above has already started. That goroutine can create indexes (a write to `b.cache`) while `TotalDocs` iterates the unlocked map, which can crash the process (see the comment on bleve.go). Also, this runs `DocCount()` over every index on each startup just to write a log line.

This is a data race: the worker goroutines all assign to the shared outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization. The race was already there, but this PR's goal is faster builds with higher concurrency, which makes it more likely to cause problems. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter. `go test -race` should catch this.

The whole `Init` now runs synchronously inside the constructor. That includes lifecycle/DB init, building the search index for every namespace, and starting the watcher.

What this breaks (answering the reviewer question):
1. `NewResourceServer` is called during wire/DI wiring (`unified.ProvideUnifiedStorageClient` → `sql.NewResourceServer`, `DashboardStorage.NewStore`, `apistore.NewRESTOptionsGetter*`). Grafana startup now blocks until the full index is built, with no timeout.
2. `Init` runs on `s.ctx`, which comes from `context.Background()`. When `sql/service.start(ctx)` is called under dskit, its ctx is ignored, so the service can't be cancelled or shut down during a long index build.
3. If `Init` fails, the server is discarded without calling `s.cancel()` or stopping the lifecycle (the DB backend stays open), and the search watch goroutine started in `search.init` leaks.
4. Any `Init` error is now a hard startup failure for all of Grafana, even when unified storage is only used for one resource. Before, only those requests failed.

Consider running the index build in the background with a readiness flag or health check, or at least passing the caller's ctx and cleaning up on error.

With every `s.Init(ctx)` check removed from the handlers, `initErr` is never consulted after construction. `Stop()` still sets `s.initErr = "service is stopping"/"service is stopped"`, but Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/IsHealthy keep serving after `Stop`, using a cancelled `s.ctx` and a stopped backend and broadcaster. The previous contract, where calls after Stop returned an error, is broken. `IsHealthy` in particular should now report the stopped state. Keep a cheap `initErr` check (e.g. an atomic/stopped flag) in the handlers, or at least in `IsHealthy`.

The ordering changed so that the search index is built before `initWatcher`. The index build can take a long time, and during it the broadcaster is nil. Also, `search.init` only subscribes to `WatchWriteEvents` after all builds finish. Any writes committed while the index is being built (from other replicas or clients of the same DB) are therefore missing from the index until they are modified again. Subscribe to events before building, or record the RV and catch up afterwards.

This skips an integration test for postgres entirely instead of fixing it. The failure appeared with this PR, probably because eager `Init` now touches the DB and builds indexes in the constructor, so the target takes longer or fails to start in CI. That is exactly the startup-behaviour change the PR description asks about, so skipping the test hides the risk. Please investigate before merging, or open a tracking issue.
